name: Transformers & attention
summary: The architecture behind modern language models: stacked layers in which every token can look back at earlier tokens and pull in what's relevant.

D1.guide: Read the sentence slowly. Which word does 'it' point back to?
text: Read this: “The cat sat on the mat because it was tired.” You know “it” means the cat, not the mat.
Attention is how the AI works that out: for each word it looks back at the earlier words and decides which ones matter most.

A transformer is a stack of identical **layers**. Each layer has two parts: **attention**, which mixes in information from other positions, and a **feed-forward network**, which processes each position on its own.

In attention, each position asks a question (a *query*), compares it with a label on every earlier position (its *key*), and takes a weighted blend of what those positions carry (their *values*). Many attention heads do this in parallel, looking for different patterns.
In models that generate text, a **causal mask** stops any position from looking ahead at tokens that haven't been written yet.

diagram.caption: One transformer layer, repeated dozens of times

D2.analogyBreaks: You highlight a few words once. Attention gives every earlier token some weight, dozens of heads do it at once in every layer, and the result is spread across many layers rather than one clear highlight.

predict.question: In a model that generates text, can a token pay attention to words that come after it?
options: No: a causal mask hides later tokens
predict.explanation: While generating, later tokens don't exist yet, and during training a mask hides them so the model learns to predict without peeking.

text: Each word builds a **query** (what it is looking for) and a **key** (what it offers). The query is compared with the keys of earlier words using a dot product, and softmax turns those scores into **attention weights** that add up to 100%.
A transformer runs many **heads** side by side. Each head has its own queries and keys, so each looks for something different. Choose a word, then switch heads and watch where its attention goes.

heads.name: Who is "it"?
heads.about: Looks for the animal a word could be about. Only "it", "was" and "tired" ask strongly; the other words have weak queries and spread out.

heads.name: Previous word
heads.about: Ignores meaning. Built only from word positions, so each word looks at the one just before it.

heads.name: Any noun
heads.about: Every word looks for nouns. It cannot tell "cat" from "mat", so "it" splits its attention between them.

interactiveConfig.note: Illustrative heads: we hand-set small query and key vectors so each head shows one pattern. The weights are real softmax arithmetic on those vectors, not read from a trained model.

tasks: In the “Who is it?” head, choose “it”. Which earlier word gets the most weight?
Switch to “Any noun” with “it” still chosen. Why is the weight now split between “cat” and “mat”?
Switch to “Previous word” and step through the sentence with the arrow keys. What does every word look at?

predict.question: When the model reads “it” in “The cat sat on the mat because it was tired”, which words can “it” pay attention to?
options: Every word in the sentence, including “was” and “tired”
“it” itself and the words before it
Only the word just before it
predict.explanation: The causal mask hides later words, so “it” can only look back. It gives every earlier word some weight; a good head puts most of it on “cat”.

text: Stack every token's query into a matrix **Q**, its key into **K** and its value into **V**. Attention is **softmax(QKᵀ ÷ √d) · V**, where *d* is the length of each query and key.

Row *i* of QKᵀ holds the dot product of token *i*'s query with every key. Dividing by √d stops the scores growing just because the vectors are longer. The **causal mask** sets scores for later tokens to −∞ so softmax gives them zero weight. Each output row is a weighted blend of the value vectors.
Edit the vectors below; every table is computed live from the formula.

interactiveConfig.note: Illustrative 2-number vectors for a cut-down sentence. Real models learn vectors with 64 to 128 numbers per head.

tasks: Look at the row for “it”. Why does its output come out close to the value of “cat”?
Change the first number of the key for “mat” from 0.4 to 2.5. What happens to the weight “it” gives to “cat”?
Turn the causal mask off. Which rows change, and which row stays the same?
D4.code:
def attention(Q, K, V, causal=True):
    d = Q.shape[-1]                      # length of each query and key
    scores = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d)           # one score for every (query, key) pair
    if causal:
        scores[j > i] = -inf             # hide tokens that come later
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)   # each row adds up to 1
    return weights @ V                   # blend the values

# multi-head: run several of these with different learned Q, K, V
# projections, then join the outputs and mix them with one more matrix
tradeoffs: Every token is compared with every other, so the score table grows with the square of the context length.
The causal mask lets a model train on a whole sentence at once while still learning to predict each word without peeking.
More heads let a layer look for more patterns at once, but each head works with shorter vectors.
Attention weights show where a head looked, not why the model gave its answer; reading them as explanations can mislead.

text: Open problems: attention's cost grows with the square of the context length, which drives work on efficient kernels, sparse and linear attention, and hybrids with state-space layers; and interpretability research into what individual heads and layers actually compute.
